blocks.text: That the name ארבה is sometimes used generally and comprises every kind of locust, and sometimes denotes a particular species, as in Ioel I, 4. Ps. LXXVIII, 46., where it is distinguished from the other names of locusts and is mentioned only in second place, has been shown by Oedmann (Vermischte Sammlungen, fasc. 2, ch. 7, part 2, p. 91. 92.) and by Ol. Gerh. Tychsen in his commentary on the locusts mentioned in the O. T., which is appended to Ignacio de Asso's little book on locusts, translated by him from Spanish into German, p. 88 (with this title: Des Don IGNACIO DE ASSO Y DEL RIO, Königl. Spanischen General-Consuls in Holland, Abhandlung von den Heuschrecken und ihren Vertilgungsmitteln, aus dem Spanischen übersetzt, und mit einem Anhang von den biblischen Heuschrecken begleitet, von OLUF GERH. TYCHSEN, Rostock 1787, 8vo). The same had long before been the opinion of Ed. Pococke in his Commentary on Joel, ch. 1, v. 4 (translated from English into Latin, Leipzig 1695, p. 7): "The word Arbeh," he says, "which we find placed here as though it were the name of a single species, we have in Levit. XI, 22. as though comprehending various species under it; whence you may rightly conjecture that this little word is sometimes used very generally, sometimes quite specifically, وقد يطلق الواحد منها علي الجميع مجازا [wa-qad yuṭlaqu al-wāḥid minhā ʿalī al-jamīʿ majāzan], the name of one species being used (as R. Tanchum puts it) for all." Thus Pococke. If, however, ארבה is the name of a species, not only Oedmann but also Tychsen, loc. cit., holds that it signifies the Gryllus gregarius of Forsskål (Descript. Animall. p. 81.). They think the Hebrew name was given to this species from רבה, to be much, because this species occurs in great numbers and migrates in swarms. I add Forsskål's words: "The Gryllus gregarius the Arabs everywhere call Djerâd, جيراد [jīrād], and the Jews living in Yemen asserted that it is the ארבה. — — At every step I stirred up whole swarms, so great was their number in these places at that time." ארבה is also the general name of the locust for J. D. Michaelis, in Supplemm. vol. 6, p. 2228., but in Levit. XI, 22., where it is distinguished from חרגל, סלעם and חגב, it seems to him to be the locust that begins to fly after its first moult, whereas before that it creeps and lacks wings. But this opinion, which is supported neither by the agreement of the Arabic and Syriac dialects, nor by the authority of the ancient translators, nor by etymology, has been refuted at length by Tychsen (p. 62 ff. of the book cited) and Oedmann (p. 87 ff. and p. 122 ff.).

To Michaelis, in Supplemm. vol. 1, p. 249, גובי seems from its etymology to be the locust first creeping out of the earth, i.e. in its first stage, which is followed by four moults of the skin: the locust-worm that has not yet shed its skin. Against this opinion stands the agreement of the ancient translators, and the passage Nahum III, 17., where winged or full-grown locusts must be meant, as Tychsen rightly points out, p. 93; he himself interprets גובי as the gryllus migratorius of Linnaeus, but on what grounds he does not explain.

משוטא מתאמר קמצא שאפא, Moschuto is the name of the wingless locust: this Hyde quotes from a certain Syriac lexicon in his notes on Peritsol's Itinera mundi, p. 125. It is clear that the bruchus is meant, that is, the young hatched from the locust's egg before it has wings. Nor, it seems, should the καμπη [kampē] of the Greek translators be interpreted otherwise. Michaelis, in Supplemm. vol. 1, p. 290, connects ܡܫܘܛܐ with the Arabic مشط [mashaṭa], he combed, he plundered, but Tychsen, p. 86, with the Chaldee שוט, to roam about.

Michaelis, however, also defends the meaning eruca [caterpillar], loc. cit.: "Notable," he says, "and classic for this opinion is the passage of Amos in which גזם is an insect harmful to vineyards, olive groves and fig trees." But locusts are no less harmful to such crops, as we shall see below, Chapter IV. And that גזם was rightly rendered bruchus by the Chaldee and the Syriac (see note 3.) I infer from the fact that in Ioel I, 4 גזם is placed before the other names of locusts, as the one that begins the devastation of the fields, which suits the bruchus best. The most fitting sense of the Hebrew words יתר הגזם אכל הארבה here will therefore be: what the bruchus left, the gryllus gregarius ate (see note 1 above). Oedmann, too, is wholly for the bruchus, fasc. 2, ch. 6, p. 116 ff., and at the same time soundly refutes the opinion of those who take גזם for the eruca [caterpillar]. Tychsen, p. 88, interprets גזם as the gryllus cristatus of Linnaeus, on the authority of Abrah. Iaphe, a Jew of Safed.
